newsitem.title: USA: Fla. judge stays execution for electric chair trial.
newsitem.headline: Fla. judge stays execution for electric chair trial.

text.p: A man who was sentenced to die in Florida's electric chair received at least a few weeks' reprieve on Thursday while a court decides whether use of the chair is cruel and unusual punishment.

Circuit Judge A.C. Soud ordered the delay at a hearing called by the Florida Supreme Court after the electric chair, already in use for 74 years, set a convict's head on fire during an execution last month.

Leo Alexander Jones was sentenced to die for the 1981 sniper killing of Jacksonville police officer Thomas Szafranski. The execution had already been delayed from last Tuesday until Friday to allow for a hearing on the chair.

April Herrle, a spokeswoman for Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles, said a hearing on a new execution order for Jones would not occur for several weeks even if Soud decides the electric chair in its present condition as a form of capital punishment is constitutional and the stay is lifted.

Jones's family members have maintained the condition of Florida's electric chair is irrelevant to his case because they believe he is innocent. Jones confessed to the killing, but has said he did so only to keep police from beating him.
The state of the electric chair became an issue on March 25 when a bolt of flame and smoke shot from the head of convicted killer Pedro Medina as he was put to death.
The incident prompted a debate over capital punishment and death penalty opponents expressed outrage over the chair, which was built by prisoners in 1923.
